opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think honestly the answer is that we don't fully know yet. But I can give you my intuition.

So the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon is this observation that when you give a Transformer a very long context, it tends to do well at using information that's near the beginning or near the end, and it kind of underweights stuff in the middle. And part of what's surprising about that is that, in principle, attention has perfect access to every position. There's no architectural reason it can't look at token 5,000 just as easily as token 50. So the fact that it struggles seems to be more about training, about the data distribution, positional encodings, how the model learns to allocate attention, than about a hard capacity limit.

State space models are kind of the opposite situation. They have a fixed-size hidden state that you're compressing the entire history into as you go. So there's a real, hard bottleneck. You can't just go back and look at token 5,000; whatever you know about it has to have survived in that state. And so you'd naively expect a recency bias, that things at the end are remembered well and things far back get overwritten or decayed.

Now, the newer models, things like Mamba with selective state spaces, are trying to make that compression smarter. The selection mechanism lets the model decide, based on the input, what to write into the state and what to ignore. So in principle, if something important shows up in the middle, the model can choose to hold onto it. But it has to make that decision at the time it reads it, without knowing what question is coming later. That's a fundamentally different problem from attention, where you can decide retroactively what was relevant.

So I don't think state space models magically solve lost-in-the-middle. If anything, for pure retrieval tasks, like needle-in-a-haystack or associative recall, they tend to be weaker than attention, and that's been shown fairly clearly. Where I think it gets interesting is hybrids. If you have mostly SSM layers doing the cheap, long-range summarization and a few attention layers that can do precise lookup, you might get a model that has a different and maybe better profile across the context. And there are tricks too, like putting the question before the document so the model knows what to keep, which matters a lot more for a recurrent model than for a Transformer.

But I'd really frame it as: these architectures have different failure modes over long contexts, and we need better benchmarks to characterize them. Lost-in-the-middle is a Transformer-shaped finding. The SSM equivalent might look more like "forgot what it didn't know it needed," and I think understanding that tradeoff is one of the more important open questions right now.

r001.rationale: The response says SSMs do not magically solve lost-in-the-middle, but does not connect that claim to the condition that the problem arises from training.

r002.rationale: It tentatively attributes the problem to training, data distribution, positional encodings, and learned attention allocation rather than a hard architectural capacity limit.

r003.rationale: It compares SSMs with Transformers, describes their different long-context failure modes, and calls for benchmarks to characterize them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a really interesting question, and I think the honest answer is that state space models change the shape of the problem rather than making it go away.

Let me back up for a second. The lost-in-the-middle result, the Liu et al. finding, is that when you give a Transformer a long context and put the relevant information somewhere in the middle, performance drops relative to when it's at the beginning or the end. And the thing that's a little strange about that is that, architecturally, attention has no reason to prefer any position. Every token can look at every other token. So the bias is coming from training: positional encodings like RoPE, the data distribution, maybe the fact that documents tend to have important stuff up front, and a kind of recency effect that comes from how next-token prediction works.

Now with state space models, Mamba, the linear RNN family, the architecture itself is genuinely asymmetric. You have a fixed-size state that you're compressing the whole history into, and that state is being updated recurrently. So you get a very natural recency bias, because recent tokens have had fewer opportunities to be decayed or overwritten. And you also, in practice, get something like a primacy effect, because the model learns to allocate some of that state to things it saw early on. So in some sense SSMs make the U-shape more principled. It's not an artifact, it's a consequence of having a bounded memory.

The flip side is that the failure mode is different. With a Transformer, the information is still in the KV cache; the model just doesn't attend to it well. With an SSM, if the information got compressed out of the state, it's gone. There's no retrieving it. So for pure needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, I'd actually expect SSMs to be worse in the middle, not better, especially as the context gets long relative to the state size. And a lot of the empirical results back that up: the recurrent models are great at things that look like aggregation or summarization and weaker at exact copying from far back.

Where I think it gets more interesting is the hybrid direction. If you have a few attention layers mixed into a mostly-SSM stack, the SSM layers give you this efficient compressed summary of the context, and the attention layers give you a sparse lookup when you really need a specific fact. That's the Jamba-style design, and the hypothesis is that the two mechanisms can cover each other's blind spots. Whether that actually fixes the middle, I think the jury's still out. My suspicion is the positional bias is mostly a training-data and objective issue, and so you'll see it in whatever architecture you train on the same data, unless you explicitly do something about it, like permuting document order or training on tasks that require pulling from the middle.

So the short version is: SSMs don't solve lost-in-the-middle. They make the recency bias structural, they trade a soft attention failure for a hard forgetting failure, and the most promising path is probably hybrids plus training interventions, not swapping one architecture for another.

r001.rationale: It says SSMs do not solve lost-in-the-middle and that the positional bias is mostly a training-data and objective issue, so changing architecture alone would not resolve it.

r002.rationale: It tentatively attributes positional bias to training data and objective, and suggests training tasks that require retrieving information from the middle.

r003.rationale: It uses SSMs as a comparison point, contrasting their structural forgetting with Transformers’ attention failure to explain how architecture affects the problem.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an interesting question, because state space models have a very different way of carrying information through a sequence. In a Transformer, you can in principle reach back and attend directly to something in the middle of the context. But having that access doesn’t necessarily mean the model learns to use it reliably.

With a state space model, you’re compressing the history into a state as you go. That can make processing long sequences much more efficient, but it also raises a question: what information survives that compression? If there’s a detail halfway through that you don’t know is important until you see the question at the end, you have to have preserved it somehow.

So I wouldn’t assume that state space models automatically solve lost in the middle. They change the tradeoff. I’d want to distinguish being able to run on a very long sequence from being able to retrieve and use information anywhere in that sequence. Those are different capabilities, and I think that distinction is where the interesting experiments are.

r001.rationale: The response says state space models do not automatically solve the problem, but does not state that the problem would persist specifically when it arises from training.

r002.rationale: It contrasts direct Transformer access with reliable use and discusses information compression, but does not tentatively attribute the problem to training data or tasks rather than architecture.

r003.rationale: It calls for experiments distinguishing long-sequence processing from retrieval, but does not propose using an alternative architecture as a reference to understand the problem’s causes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an interesting question, because state space models approach long contexts in a pretty different way. In a Transformer, you keep the tokens around and can, in principle, attend directly to any of them. But that doesn’t mean the model actually learns to use information equally well wherever it appears—that’s the lost-in-the-middle issue.

With a state space model, you’re continually compressing what you’ve seen into a state. That gives you a really attractive computational story for long sequences, but it also creates a question: what information survives that compression? If you need to retrieve some arbitrary detail from the middle of a document, it’s not obvious that a fixed-size state makes that easier. You could trade a positional bias for a forgetting problem.

So I wouldn’t assume that being able to process a longer sequence means you’ve solved long-context retrieval. I’d want to look at what the task requires, how the model is trained, and whether it has some attention or retrieval mechanism alongside the state space component. Those combinations seem interesting, because maintaining a useful summary and looking up a specific detail are different capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says longer sequence processing does not guarantee better retrieval and notes training matters, but it does not state that state space models would fail to resolve the problem when its cause is training.

r002.rationale: It says the answer depends partly on training and task requirements, but does not tentatively identify training data and tasks, rather than architecture, as the source of lost-in-the-middle.

r003.rationale: It discusses state space models and possible attention or retrieval mechanisms, but does not propose using an alternative architecture as a reference to understand how the problem arises.
